ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Psychiatric inpatients and outpatients 18 -30 years old were recruited through the Western Psychiatric Hospital at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC).

> We recruited patients admitted for a suicide attempt (SA), participants with active suicidal ideation (SI), and psychiatric controls with no current suicidal ideation or behavior (PC).

> Healthy controls (HC) with no history of psychiatric disorders or suicidal ideation and behavior were recruited through a university participant registry.

> Participants were excluded if they had a chronic condition affecting immune or endocrine pathways, were pregnant, or taking prescribed oral corticosteroids or other medications that affect immune and neuroendocrine functioning in the past 12 months, and if they had an infection or were on antibiotics in the past two weeks.

> The study was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board and all participants provided their informed consent to participate in the study.

> We recruited a total of 515 participants of which 397 (77.1%) completed a baseline assessment.

> All participants completed the Vocabulary and Matrix Reasoning tests from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence 2nd Edition (WASI-II) 23 to estimate participants' IQ.

> For each trial, participants are presented with a "safe" cup with a fixed monetary reward on one side of the screen and 2 -5 "risky" cups that either gave no reward or a higher reward than the safe cup.

> Participants completed a battery of self-report measures assessing clinical symptoms associated with suicidality.

> HC participants were excluded from these analyses because no suicidal events were expected or occurred in this group.

> For the group by time interactions, IPW analyses adjusting for attrition showed that SA participants had a significantly greater decline in the proportion of risky choices under stress over time relative to HC (Supplementary Table 7), even when adjusting for covariates (β = -0.119, SE = 0.021, Tukey p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.534; Table 2; Figure 1).

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethics declaration-All the study methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of the institutional review board (IRB) of the University of Pittsburgh and were approved by the IRB under protocol #: STUDY19070226.

> The study was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board and all participants provided their informed consent to participate in the study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p's > 0.97", "p = 0.588", "p=0.083"), Sentence = c("Levels of IL-6 and TNFα assessed using ELLA correlate highly with those assessed by ELISA (p's > 0.97) 27 .", "In the non-IPW sensitivity analyses, the SA by time interaction for risky choices under stress was replicated (β = -0.092, SE = 0.025, Tukey p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 0.427; Supplementary Table 8), whereas the SA by time interaction for the stress-minus-neutral difference was not replicated (β = -0.024, SE = 0.019, Tukey p = 0.588, Cohen's d = 0.202; Supplementary Tables 8) .", "However, this result did not remain significant after controlling for clinical covariates (HR = 0.625, 95% CI [0.367, 1.063], p=0.083) (Supplementary Tables 14 15)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

ethics_statements: Ethics declaration-All the study methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of the institutional review board (IRB) of the University of Pittsburgh and were approved by the IRB under protocol #: STUDY19070226.
The study was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board and all participants provided their informed consent to participate in the study.
live_data_statements: Psychiatric inpatients and outpatients 18 -30 years old were recruited through the Western Psychiatric Hospital at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC).
We recruited patients admitted for a suicide attempt (SA), participants with active suicidal ideation (SI), and psychiatric controls with no current suicidal ideation or behavior (PC).
Healthy controls (HC) with no history of psychiatric disorders or suicidal ideation and behavior were recruited through a university participant registry.

Participants were excluded if they had a chronic condition affecting immune or endocrine pathways, were pregnant, or taking prescribed oral corticosteroids or other medications that affect immune and neuroendocrine functioning in the past 12 months, and if they had an infection or were on antibiotics in the past two weeks.
The study was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board and all participants provided their informed consent to participate in the study.
We recruited a total of 515 participants of which 397 (77.1%) completed a baseline assessment.
All participants completed the Vocabulary and Matrix Reasoning tests from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence 2nd Edition (WASI-II) 23 to estimate participants' IQ.

For each trial, participants are presented with a "safe" cup with a fixed monetary reward on one side of the screen and 2 -5 "risky" cups that either gave no reward or a higher reward than the safe cup.
Participants completed a battery of self-report measures assessing clinical symptoms associated with suicidality.
HC participants were excluded from these analyses because no suicidal events were expected or occurred in this group.

For the group by time interactions, IPW analyses adjusting for attrition showed that SA participants had a significantly greater decline in the proportion of risky choices under stress over time relative to HC (Supplementary Table 7), even when adjusting for covariates (β = -0.119, SE = 0.021, Tukey p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.534; Table 2; Figure 1).
